newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's Aleman faces high hopes, harsh reality.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's Aleman faces high hopes, harsh reality.

text.p: Nicaraguan President-elect Arnoldo Aleman takes power on January 10 amid a long-awaited economic recovery, but incoming officials warn real economic change will not come easy to Latin America's second poorest nation.

Nicaragua has enjoyed three consecutive years of growth and outgoing officials predict up to seven percent growth in 1997, after more than a decade of economic gloom that saw annual per capita income fall from $1,122 in 1978 to $430 in 1990.

Officials in President Violeta Chamorro's outgoing government boast the tough, free-market reforms adopted by Chamorro in 1990 after she toppled the Marxist Sandinista government at the ballot box are finally paying dividends.
Despite the rebound, Nicaragua remains the poorest country in Latin America after Haiti, and 52 percent of Nicaraguans are underemployed.
"After five years, I can say with complete responsibility that we are an emerging country, with a future, and the ability to grow," Central Bank President Evenor Taboada said.
And the numbers seem to back him up.

From 1990 to 1996, inflation fell from 13,490 percent to 10.8 percent, the foreign debt was cut from $10.6 billion to about $3.8 billion, the economy went from a 0.2 percent decline to 5.5 percent growth and exports soared from $340 million to $710 million, according to official figures.
But tough problems remain, and officials in Aleman's future right-wing government warned against premature euphoria.

"There is a lot of fantasy in these predictions of seven percent and the future. We are clear that we are inheriting a very delicate situation," Francisco "Che" Lainez, Aleman's future Economy Minister, told Reuters.

Lainez, who founded and directed Nicaragua's Central Bank in the 1960s under former dictator Anastasio Somoza, said the problems his government will inherit include high budget and trade deficits, run-down infrastructure, and property disputes inherited from the Sandinista era.
The Chamorro government financed the deficits with abundant foreign aid instead of correcting the imbalances, and foreign aid will fall in the coming years, he warned.
But perhaps the major challenge facing Aleman will be convincing investors that Nicaragua, wracked by decades of civil war, is a stable place to invest, economists said.
"Foreign investment is not going to come immediately...I think it will come after Aleman completes his first year in office," Alegria said.

Aleman's ability to produce economic growth may hinge on making peace with the Sandinistas, who aside from holding some 40 percent of the seats in the next National Assembly, control many city councils, the army, police and trade unions, Alegria noted.

Despite the end of its bloody, eight-year civil war and return of the free market in 1990, Nicaraguan remains bitterly polarized between the left-wing Sandinistas and the right wing, currently represented by Aleman's Liberal Alliance coalition.

Foreign investors fear instability following former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega's refusal to accept the legitimacy of Aleman's November 20 election victory, and will wait a year to see how events unfold, said economist Mario Alegria.
Lainez said the incoming government's economic priorities will be agriculture and tourism, rebuilding Nicaragua's damaged infrastructure and attracting companies to its free trade zone.
